title: The day I stopped running
text: When I was seventeen I was convinced that rest was something other people needed. My coach, a quiet man who rarely raised his voice, had written one day off into my weekly plan, and I treated it like a clerical error. Every Sunday I laced up my trainers anyway and ran the river loop, partly out of stubbornness, and partly because I could not bear the thought that a rival somewhere was gaining ground while I lay on the sofa.

For a few months it seemed to work, which is the cruel part. My times dropped, my friends admired my discipline, and I wore my tiredness like a medal. Then, in March, I began to notice small things. My legs felt heavy on the stairs. I woke before the alarm and could not get back to sleep, yet I dragged myself through lessons in a fog. Worse, the running that had once cleared my head now felt like paying off a debt.

Looking back, the strangest thing is how reasonable it all felt at the time. Nobody around me suggested that I was doing anything wrong; on the contrary, my parents were proud of my routine, my classmates teased me about my 'iron will', and my phone filled up with photographs of other teenagers who seemed to train every single day. Not one of them posted a picture of a rest day, and so I assumed such days simply did not exist for anyone serious.

I did what many young athletes do: I blamed everything except the obvious cause. Exams, I told myself. A cold, the weather, a bad batch of pasta. When my coach suggested a week of easy jogging, I nodded politely and ran harder behind his back, a decision I now find almost comic. It all came to a head at the regional trials, where I started well, **hit a wall** at the halfway mark and finished almost a minute behind my own best time.

The doctor who examined me afterwards was kind but unsparing. My resting heart rate was unusually high and my iron level was low, and my body, she said, had been sending signals for weeks, only I had not been listening. She did not forbid sport; she asked me to do something far harder, which was to do less of it. Two weeks of walking and sleeping felt like a punishment, and I resented every hour, until I noticed that the heaviness in my legs was beginning to lift.

What surprised me most was that recovery was not a pause in training but a part of it. When I returned, I was slower for a fortnight, then noticeably quicker than before. My coach, to his credit, never said 'I told you so'. He simply moved the rest day to a different place in the week, as though nothing had happened, and left me to draw my own conclusions. It was the most useful piece of coaching I ever received, and he never once raised the subject.

I am not suggesting that talent can do without effort; it cannot, and anyone who tells you otherwise is selling something. But I have come to think that the ability to stop is every bit as valuable as the willingness to push. These days, when the old guilt creeps in on a day off, I remind myself that the athletes who last longest are seldom the ones who train hardest, only the ones who have learnt to listen to their own bodies, however loudly the voice inside them insists otherwise.

questions.q: Why did the author run on her rest day?
options: She wanted to please her coach.
She feared that other runners would overtake her.
She had no other free time.

questions.q: What does 'it' in 'For a few months it seemed to work' refer to?
options: Her habit of resting on Sundays.

questions.q: 'Hit a wall' in paragraph 4 means that the author …
How did the author react to her coach's advice about easy jogging?
options: She pretended to agree but ignored it.
She asked the doctor for her opinion.

questions.q: What did the doctor ask the author to do?
options: Stop all sport for a month.

questions.q: Which fact is NOT mentioned in the text?
options: The author's heart rate was high.
The author lost her place in the team.
The author's times improved at first.
talent is more important than effort.
coaches should plan more rest days.
knowing when to stop is important.
